He has 10 years of experience writing for print and digital platforms and has worked at The New York Times, NDTV and The Indian Express in the past. Europe's biggest gas supplier battling cyberattack – with no timeline for recovery
articles.text:
Norwegian energy giant Equinor is battling a cyberattack on its IT systems, though the company insists that hackers haven't disrupted its oil and gas production.

Equinor, Europe's largest supplier of natural gas, first disclosed the attack on Tuesday evening, saying it had called in the relevant resources to deal with the intrusion and had found no indication that any data had been stolen.

In an update on Wednesday, the company said it had a better handle on how the attack was carried out and which of its systems had been compromised, though it stopped short of sharing either of those details.

"As this is not a virus attack, there is no risk of the attack spreading," Equinor said. The company added that it had found nothing to suggest the incident would affect employees, partners, or suppliers.

In a further update on Thursday, Equinor said the attack remained ongoing but did not appear to be specifically targeting the company. Production continued normally, with no indications that data had been stolen or altered. The incident has been reported to police.

What kind of attack Equinor is dealing with remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified those responsible, disclosed whether it's received any demands from the hackers, or said when it expects the affected systems to be fully restored.

The Register has asked Equinor to elaborate, including whether any of its UK operations have been affected and whether the hackers managed to venture beyond its corporate IT network.

Equinor spokesperson Ellen Maria Skjelsbæk told Norwegian news agency NTB that the company hadn't lost access to its IT systems, though staff could have trouble accessing some corporate applications and services. Email appears to be among the casualties, with Reuters reporting that the company's internal email system was down.

Equinor, which traded as Statoil until 2018, is still largely in the hands of the Norwegian state, which owns 67 percent of the company. The oil and gas biz employs around 25,000 people and operates in more than 20 countries.

The bulk of Equinor's oil and gas production takes place off the coast of Norway, but the company also pumps oil and gas in the UK, US, Brazil, and Canada. It's one of the companies behind Dogger Bank, the enormous offshore wind project off England's northeast coast, and is also in the business of capturing and storing carbon dioxide.

Equinor's assurances about production will be particularly welcome in Europe, which has become increasingly reliant on Norwegian gas since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The attack comes just weeks after Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) raised its cyberattack risk assessment to four on a five-point scale. The agency said the number of successful cyber operations against Norwegian businesses had tripled over the preceding six months and warned of potential disruption to essential services, including water and electricity supplies.

Europe has already had a few nasty reminders this year of what happens when hackers get their hands on industrial equipment. Last week, the French government pinned a series of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems at more than 700 retail sites in October on a hacking unit affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The crooks turned up the temperature in supermarket fridges and freezers, ruining tens of millions of euros' worth of food and starting fires at some premises.

Nothing suggests Equinor's hackers have similar ambitions, or that they've got anywhere near the kit used to extract and transport oil and gas. Given how much of Europe depends on that kit continuing to work, a little more detail from the Norwegian energy giant wouldn't go amiss. ®

India expects to finalise trade deals with EU, US in coming months, says Piyush Goyal
Commerce minister Piyush Goyal says India expects to finalise free trade agreements with the European Union and the US in the coming months.
India is expected to finalise free trade agreements (FTAs) with the European Union and the US in the next few months, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal said on Wednesday, urging Indian industry to leverage the country’s growing economic strength to make the world dependent on India.
Addressing the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Ficci) on the occasion of its centenary, Goyal said India’s ambition should go beyond self-reliance and focus on building capabilities that make it indispensable to global markets.
“When Prime Minister Modi talks about ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat’, in a way the idea has come a full circle from ‘Swadeshi’ which inspired Ficci 100 years ago,” he said, referring to the federation’s origins in the Swadeshi movement.
“Swadeshi to Atmanirbhar, both mean the same,” Goyal said, asking the industry to aspire beyond self-reliance. “Today, I would like to suggest going one step forward. We need to make the world dependent upon us,” he said.
Goyal cited India’s expanding trade influence through recent FTAs, saying the country had finalised nine such agreements in the past four-and-a-half years with 38 developed countries, representing a combined GDP of $60 trillion. Including FTAs concluded before 2014, India has preferential market access to economies with a combined GDP of nearly $70 trillion, with another $15 trillion to be added in the near future, he said.
“We need to create leverage in India, and we have the capabilities. We have the talent. Today, we have capital. Today, we have entrepreneurs. Today, we have the skill sets. Today, we have a robust economic situation to help us forward. We have a strong banking ecosystem. And, therefore, our ambition has to be higher,” he added.
Goyal said India and its industry were capable of taking on bigger challenges, pointing to record exports of $90 billion in October despite ongoing wars and geopolitical turbulence.
He recalled setting an export target for 2026-27 in consultation with industry, even as the International Monetary Fund had projected global trade growth of about 1.9% for the year. India set an ambitious target of $1 trillion in exports in FY27, requiring annual growth of 16%, after recording exports of goods and services worth $863 billion in FY26.
“I had two choices before me… [I could have said], Oh, world is going to grow at 1.9%. We will grow at 5%. And let’s set a target of $900 billion,” he said. “I would have got enough kudos for that [for setting up an easy goal],” he said. “But the whole team, and that includes all of you… were willing to go along with me when I suggested, let’s [aim] for a trillion dollar exports this year,” he added.
Goyal said India had achieved exports worth $570 billion in the first seven months of FY27 and expressed confidence that it would reach the remaining $430 billion target in the next five months. “When you really desire something from the heart, it happens,” he said.

articles.text:
Man accused in Andhra chainsaw attack discharged from hospital, girl shows signs of recovery
The 21-year-old accused in the chainsaw attack on a Class 10 girl in Andhra Pradesh was discharged from hospital and taken back to jail after his health improved.
The 21-year-old man accused of attacking a Class 10 student with a chainsaw at Zilla Parishad High School in Rapthadu, Andhra Pradesh’s Anantapur district, was discharged from the Kurnool Government General Hospital, police said on Thursday.
Doctors said on Wednesday that Hemanth alias Dummu, who was shot at by police while allegedly attempting to escape custody, was discharged following improvement in his health condition.
“He responded well to treatment and his health parameters were now normal. His blood pressure, pulse rate and electrocardiogram (ECG) reports were all within normal limits, indicating that he had recovered sufficiently,” Kurnool hospital superintendent Dr K Venkateshwarlu said.
The doctors submitted their medical report to the judge of the local court in the afternoon, following which the police took Hemanth back to Anantapur, where he was lodged in Reddipalli jail, a police officer said.
Hemanth had allegedly entered the school premises carrying a chainsaw and attacked the student on October 31.
Doctors at Manipal Hospital in Bengaluru informed the state government that the girl, who suffered serious injuries, was showing significant signs of recovery.
State minister for education and information technology Nara Lokesh said in a statement that he had held a video conference with the medical team at Manipal Hospital in Bengaluru in the morning to review the health condition of the 15-year-old girl. “Her major wounds had healed and the stitches had been removed, while treatment for a few minor injuries was continuing... Her confidence was gradually returning, they added, describing her as a fighter who had displayed extraordinary courage during her battle for survival,” he said.
Hours after he was caught in the Atmakur forests on November 1, Hemanth was being taken to Rapthadu for a reconstruction of the crime scene when he allegedly tried to flee and hurled stones at the police personnel escorting him.
“When the police were bringing him to Raptadu to reconstruct the scene of the offence he had committed at the school, he tried to escape and started hurling stones at the police personnel. Several police personnel sustained injuries in the attack, when they tried to overpower him,” an officer said.
Hemanth was initially admitted to the Anantapur government hospital for treatment, where his right leg was amputated.
The Anantapur police shifted Hemanth on November 13 following the deterioration of his health condition. The medical team at the Anantapur hospital submitted a status report to the high court stating that the blood clots in his blood vessels could pose a serious threat to his life if not treated immediately.
The clots could travel to vital organs, including the heart, brain and lungs, potentially resulting in fatal complications. The medical team said that the Anantapur hospital lacked the necessary infrastructure, including a heart-lung machine and other specialised facilities required to remove the clots.
After obtaining permission from the court, the police shifted him to Kurnool Government General Hospital in an Armed Reserve (AR) escort vehicle, accompanied by around 10 police personnel.
Kurnool hospital superintendent Dr Venkateshwarlu said, “We provided all necessary medical treatment in accordance with the court’s directions and that the accused was declared medically fit for discharge.”

articles.title: European Commission scrambles to contain AI-assisted cyberattack
articles.text:
The European Commission is picking up the pieces after hackers wielding an AI-powered security testing tool targeted its internal IT systems, potentially exposing staff members' personal data.

The attack, first reported by Politico, has caused more than 10 days of disruption at the EU's executive arm. Among the applications temporarily taken offline were Sysper, which staff use to access payslips, submit timesheets, and request vacation time, and MyPMO, which handles medical reimbursements.

Both were brought back online earlier this week, though Sysper fell over again on Wednesday. The Commission's translation services were also affected.

"The European Commission has taken the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign," Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told Politico. "Individual systems were targeted and, in line with our standard practice, we have informed those concerned."

According to Politico's sources, the Commission's cybersecurity defenders detected hackers using ARTEX, a publicly available AI-powered penetration testing framework. The incident prompted an emergency meeting of the Commission's Corporate Management Board earlier this month, and tech commissioner Henna Virkkunen briefed her fellow commissioners on Wednesday.

The Commission has yet to respond to The Register's questions about the attack, including whether the crooks got their hands on employee data or whether the applications were simply taken offline as a precaution.

The attack might not come as much of a surprise to the Commission's own security bods. CERT-EU, which looks after the cybersecurity of EU institutions, warned on November 5 that it had spotted what it believed to be ARTEX-assisted attacks against organizations under its watch.

The developer behind ARTEX pulled the project's GitHub repository in October after reports that hackers were putting the software to use. But by then, the code was out in the wild, and anyone wanting to have a crack at an organization's IT estate could get hold of one of several forks.

The FBI also sounded the alarm last week [PDF], revealing that researchers had found more than 1,600 ARTEX consoles exposed to the internet. In some of the attacks detailed by the Feds, hackers went from identifying a target to obtaining privileged access in less than three hours.

“What used to take a skilled operator days or weeks of chaining is now happening in hours because frameworks like ARTEX let a single actor stand up fleets of agents that plan, probe, exploit, and move laterally with almost no further human input after the initial goal is set,” Snehal Antani, CEO of security firm Horizon3.ai, told The Register.

Antani said the proliferation of these tools could also make life harder for investigators trying to establish who's behind an attack, as government-backed hackers and garden-variety cybercriminals increasingly draw from the same toolbox.

Commission staff at least appear to have been paid on time. According to Politico, some couldn't book time off or submit their timesheets, but salaries landed as usual. Whether the hackers managed to snoop on their payslips is something the Commission has yet to establish. ®
articles.summary:
The European Commission is picking up the pieces after hackers wielding an AI-powered security testing tool targeted its internal IT systems, potentially exposing staff members' personal data.

Union demands Capita lose Whitehall payroll deal after pensions fiasco
articles.text:
The Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS) is campaigning to scrap Capita's Whitehall shared services contract, citing the outsourcer's troubled handling of civil service pensions.

The Synergy deal, which Capita values at £370 million, covers HR, payroll, finance, and other back-office services across four government departments and nearly 100 arm's-length bodies. PCS wants the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), which leads the program, to bring the work in-house.

In a statement shared on X, the union pointed to Capita's troubled administration of the separate Civil Service Pension Scheme, which has left thousands of retirees struggling to access payments.

"The ongoing Capita pensions scandal has left civil servants facing financial hardship, distress and uncertainty. Now MPs are raising serious questions about the government's decision to award Capita the Synergy contract, putting the company in charge of vital payroll and HR services affecting more than 250,000 civil servants," the statement said.

"How many more warnings does the government need? In Parliament, MPs have challenged Capita's record, highlighted the devastating consequences of pension administration failures and questioned the wisdom of handing the company even greater responsibility.

"PCS has warned for years about the dangers of outsourcing essential public services. We need accountability. We need answers. And we need a government that puts public servants before private profit. Stop the Capita Synergy contract. Bring these vital services back in-house."

The union has also launched an online petition backing its campaign. Capita has been offered the opportunity to comment.

On Tuesday in Parliament, Labour MP Andy McDonald said the stakes were high. "Civil servants must be paid correctly and on time. Payroll failures can mean missed mortgage payments, rent arrears and serious financial hardship. The failures in Capita's administration of civil service pensions demonstrate what can happen when essential services are outsourced and they go wrong," he said.

He called on the government to conduct an urgent review of the decision to continue outsourcing Synergy's essential administrative services with "a proper assessment of how and when they could be brought back into public provision."

DWP minister Lilian Greenwood responded that Capita's appointment followed a two-year procurement supported by commercial, legal, and program delivery experts. "Functional experts from all four Departments evaluated the final bids. The procurement met regulatory requirements, with advice from His Majesty's Treasury and the Cabinet Office, and passed their required controls," she said.

"Because this is a critical service, the program did not simply choose the cheapest option. Evaluation was weighted 70 percent on quality and 30 percent on cost.

"The program did consider insourcing the whole service or parts of it. However, its business case and approvals concluded that continuing to outsource business process services was the most efficient and cost-effective option for Departments, Government and taxpayers."

articles.text:
India-Japan 2+2 dialogue: Both sides push defence, technology and maritime cooperation
At the fourth India-Japan 2+2 dialogue in Tokyo, the two sides agreed to deepen defence, maritime security, AI and technology cooperation.
India and Japan pledged to uphold a free and open world order in an “increasingly severe” global security environment and to deepen cooperation in key areas such as defence, technology, economic security, digital connectivity and security of AI systems as their defence and foreign ministers held their fourth 2+2 dialogue in Tokyo on Thursday.
Defence minister Rajnath Singh and external affairs minister S Jaishankar’s talks with their Japanese counterparts, Shinjiro Koizumi and Toshimitsu Motegi, also led to progress in efforts to deepen cooperation on air and space domain awareness, a proposed information-sharing agreement, and collaboration on underwater and missile technologies.
The 2+2 meeting, held hours before a summit of the leaders of China, Russia and the US in Shenzhen, produced a joint statement that, without directly referring to China, opposed all attempt to unilaterally change the status quo, expressed grave concerns over economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions and non-market policies and practices, and backed a fair competitive global environment and resilient and reliable supply chains.
“This is an important relationship for peace and prosperity in the Indo-Pacific region,” Singh told a joint media interaction. Besides calling for early consideration of agreements related to the transfer of Japan’s Unified Complex Radio Antenna (Unicorn) system to the Indian Navy, Singh pressed for the early conclusion of a maritime ship repair arrangement and reciprocal provision of ship repair facilities between the two sides.
The ministers affirmed that India and Japan share a common responsibility to uphold a free and open global order based on rule of law in “an increasingly severe international security environment”, Japan’s foreign ministry said. Motegi said the two countries should serve as “an anchor for regional stability”, particularly in the Indo-Pacific, as the global security environment becomes increasingly uncertain.
Jaishankar said the value of the trusted India-Japan partnership has increased at a time when the world order is facing multiple shocks, including two major conflicts, growing economic volatility and concerns about energy, trade, food and health security. Noting that the two countries are strong proponents of reformed multilateralism and committed to keeping the Indo-Pacific free and open, he said: “The big picture that our cooperation seeks to support is a multipolar Asia and a multipolar world.”
“We also spoke about a growing tendency to weaponise connectivity, resources, services, supply chains and market shares. Many of these have direct implications for our national security,” Jaishankar said, adding that India-Japan maritime cooperation can ensure that maritime trade functions smoothly as connectivity and chokepoints are impacted by the West Asia conflict.
A significant outcome of the meeting was the decision to accelerate coordination for the early realisation of a letter of intent (LOI) for the use of India’s firing ranges by Japan’s Self-Defence Forces to conduct live fire training, including the use of surface-to-ship missiles, the joint statement said. The two sides also agreed to further deepen cooperation in bilateral exercises by making them more complex, integrating unmanned systems and pursuing bilateral and multilateral drills at short notice.
The two sides expressed their expectation for the early formulation of arrangements related to the transfer of the Unicorn system, including the finalisation of the “Acceptance of Necessity” by India by February 2027. The two sides will also work to strengthen defence industrial cooperation under the framework of “Design with Japan, Make in India”.
Under the recently signed memorandum of arrangement on maritime security cooperation, the two sides agreed to focus on concrete outcomes between the Indian Navy and Japan’s Maritime Self-Defence Force in maritime and air domain awareness, search and rescue and information-sharing. Defence authorities will also work to enhance mine countermeasures capabilities and explore joint development in naval shipbuilding and design, the joint statement said.
The two sides further agreed to hold a dialogue between their consular authorities to discuss a range of consular-related matters, including holding a table-top exercise on cooperation in helping Indian and Japanese nationals abroad.
As part of efforts to strengthen secure and resilient digital connectivity in the Indo-Pacific, they agreed to enhance bilateral cooperation in developing trusted, redundant and high-speed undersea cable networks and to share best practices on the security, reliability and resilience of critical undersea communications infrastructure.
Following an increase in cyber attacks, the ministers agreed to strengthen cybersecurity cooperation, including in AI-enabled cybersecurity and security of AI systems. They directed their teams to renew the existing memorandum of cooperation in cybersecurity and convene the next edition of the India-Japan Cyber Dialogue at an early date.
The joint statement said the two sides strongly condemned all forms of terrorism and violent extremism, including cross-border terror, and sought concerted actions against all UN-listed terror groups such as al-Qaeda, Daesh, Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammad and their proxies.
Motegi and Koizumi explained Japan’s ongoing efforts to revise its National Security Strategy, National Defence Strategy and Defence Buildup Program, which they said will contribute to enhanced cooperation with India to maintain peace and security in the region and beyond.

articles.title: Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things
articles.text:
There's something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it's the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watched other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn't watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature.

The team randomly assigned male mice to three groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training with three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them.

The ninth day was "fight night," when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents' excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously.

articles.text:
Qualcomm has opened cloud-based trials of its Dragonfly AI200 rack-scale inference system to selected customers through Cirrascale Cloud Services.

Dragonfly AI200 is Qualcomm's pitch for running large language, multimodal, and other AI models without Nvidia-sized power and operating bills.

Whether it delivers those savings is something customers can now put to the test on Cirrascale's AI Innovation Cloud, with a route into production deployments, Qualcomm says. Cirrascale also demonstrated the system at SC26 in Chicago on November 17-18.

The AI200 is part of Qualcomm's Dragonfly datacenter lineup, which also includes the AI250 and AI300 accelerators and the C1000 server CPU. The company set out its broader ambitions at its Investor Day in June.

Each AI200 accelerator card carries 768 GB of LPDDR memory, with 56 cards providing about 43 TB in a liquid-cooled rack. Qualcomm says the system supports models ranging from 7 billion to 10 trillion parameters, including long-context, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic workloads.

As we previously explored, packing in memory doesn't necessarily mean matching Nvidia's performance. Its Blackwell-based NVL72 systems use fast – and costly – HBM3e stacks, while Qualcomm has opted for LPDDR, more commonly found in mobile devices.

"AI inference is becoming one of the largest and most important computing workloads in the datacenter, and the industry needs a more efficient approach," said Tony Pialis, Qualcomm's executive vice president and general manager for datacenter.

He claimed that the AI200 brings the company's experience with high-performance, low-power computing to a rack-scale infrastructure, in an architecture designed around the performance, memory, and cost requirements of inference workloads.

"Our customers need efficient, scalable infrastructure that can support increasingly sophisticated models without allowing power and operating costs to become the limiting factor," said Cirrascale CEO Dave Driggers.

"By working with Qualcomm, we can give customers evaluation access to a compelling new architecture purpose-built for the next generation of AI inference."

The chip firm also has its own software stack, the Dragonfly AI Infrastructure Management Suite, for provisioning, monitoring, workload orchestration, and fault handling across rack-scale deployments. ®

Voyager 1 celebrates one light-day with a nice lie-down
articles.text:
Voyager 1 marked its milestone of one light-day from Earth in time-honored fashion: by giving controllers the silent treatment.

On November 14, the mission team noticed that the veteran spacecraft had stopped returning science and engineering data. A Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra, Australia, picked up its carrier signal, but no data.

The carrier signal indicates that Voyager 1 can still keep its antenna pointed at Earth and operate its transmitting equipment. However, something could be amiss with the system responsible for collecting and collating data from the spacecraft.

Something similar happened in 2023. After a few months of troubleshooting, engineers managed to coax a response from the probe, and by June 2024, NASA was delighted to announce that the spacecraft was back in action.

The problem was traced to a faulty computer chip, and engineers devised a software update to work around the defective hardware. That experience will stand the team in good stead this time around.

There was also a brief interruption in communications with Voyager 1 in October, which could have been caused by the spacecraft dropping into safe mode after a thruster failover occurred. Engineers are investigating whether the two incidents are connected.

The Voyagers have an impressive amount of fault protection built in, which has contributed to their extraordinary longevity. It will be half a century in 2027 since the spacecraft were launched, so glitches are understandable and likely.

NASA expects to confirm on November 19 that Voyager 1 was still operating when it reached one light-day from Earth on November 18, using its carrier signal and trajectory calculations. The day's delay neatly illustrates a major headache for engineers: communication latency.

It now takes more than 24 hours for commands to reach the spacecraft, and the same amount of time for a response to be received. Diagnosing the fault could therefore take weeks or longer. ®

Former Karnataka chief minister Siddaramaiah on Thursday clarified why he was seated in the fifth row during the launch of Sonia Gandhi's memoir Belonging in Delhi on November 16, dismissing claims that he was being sidelined in Congress.

Odisha evacuates 1.05 lakh people ahead of Cyclone Akvan, deploys 295 rescue teams
Cyclone Akvan is expected to make landfall near Gopalpur by Friday noon, with winds reaching 110 kmph. Odisha has shifted over 1 lakh people to shelters
Odisha has evacuated more than 1.05 lakh people ahead of Cyclone Akvan, which is expected to make landfall near Gopalpur in Ganjam district by noon on Friday, as the state government steps up preparations to minimise casualties, chief secretary Anu Garg said on Thursday.
Garg said that 60 Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force (ODRAF) teams, 14 National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams and 221 fire service teams had been deployed for rescue and relief operations.
She added that 1.05 lakh people had so far been shifted to 1,224 shelters across the state, and the evacuation drive was continuing. Ganjam accounted for the highest number of evacuations at 45,364, followed by Gajapati with 18,000 people.
Deep Dive
“The goal is zero casualty and whatever is required to achieve it will be done. District collectors have been asked to err on the side of caution. Even if a district is in the yellow zone and not in the red, they should assume the worst. Hope for the best, but be prepared for the worst,” Garg said.
She said the India Meteorological Department (IMD) had predicted that the cyclone would cross the coast around Gopalpur by noon on Friday, bringing winds of 90-100 kmph, gusting up to 110 kmph.
Residents of villages in landslide-prone areas of Gajapati and Kandhamal districts, particularly those situated along the foothills, were being shifted to safer locations. The administration had identified 6,109 vulnerable locations and was evacuating residents from these areas.
IMD director general Mrutyunjay Mohapatra said Cyclone Akvan was moving towards the Odisha coast at around 15 kmph, considerably faster than its speed of just 3 kmph on Wednesday morning.
Unlike Cyclone Arnab, which moved relatively slowly over the sea, Akvan had gained speed due to the strengthening influence of an anticyclone over or near Myanmar in the eastern Bay of Bengal, he said.
“The system was moving under favourable atmospheric conditions and was likely to maintain its intensity over the next 24 hours. However, it is not expected to intensify significantly further as dry and cold air approaching from northwestern India could interfere with its core circulation,” Mohapatra said.
Mohapatra, however, cautioned that the weakening of the system after landfall would not lessen the threat, as extremely heavy rainfall, flash floods and urban inundation could cause widespread damage. “Isolated places could receive 20-30 cm of rainfall,” he said, adding that several districts, from Ganjam and Gajapati to Balasore and Mayurbhanj, could experience heavy to very heavy rainfall.
The Rushikulya, Vansadhara and Nagavali rivers, besides the lower Mahanadi, could witness rising water levels, while urban flooding and waterlogging in low-lying areas remained major concerns. The districts likely to face flash flood risk included Jagatsinghpur, Kendrapada, Bhadrak, Balasore, Mayurbhanj, Keonjhar and Jajpur.
Meanwhile, officials have imposed restrictions on tourist activities along the state’s coastline as a precautionary measure. Visitors have been barred from Puri beach and other coastal destinations, including Konark, Chandrabhaga, Astaranga and Baliharachandi. Tourists have been advised to stay away from beaches.
Visits to the Konark Sun Temple have also been prohibited in view of the prevailing weather conditions. Boat services and other watercraft operations have been suspended in the Konark and Astaranga areas.
Boating services at Satapada in Chilika Lake have also been stopped, along with ferry services for public transportation. Fishermen have been prohibited from taking their boats into the lake.

articles.title: Microsoft To Do will soon become Microsoft Done
articles.text:
Microsoft has slipped some bad news into this week's Ignite AI puffery: the To Do apps are retiring on June 30, 2027, ending a journey that began with its acquisition of Wunderlist more than a decade ago.

The confirmation came in an announcement about unified tasks and plans for Copilot and Microsoft 365. Until now, there was To Do or Planner (in basic or premium guise). The idea is "a single system for tracking your work as an individual, as a team, and as an organization." To Do contributes features to that future, but its apps don't get to join it.

The problem is that Planner doesn't do everything To Do does. Microsoft would like users to migrate to Planner but, by the company's own admission, there are plenty of gaps. No native Windows or Mac desktop apps are planned to replace To Do; file attachments aren't supported on tasks in the Planner private plan, and there's no equivalent to To Do list groups in Planner. "Equivalent To Do printing and email-list capabilities are not currently planned for the replacement experience," and so on.

Existing To Do tasks and lists won't migrate to Planner either. They'll remain accessible through Planner until June 30, 2027, but that access ends with the apps. Microsoft says the date does not itself trigger deletion of the underlying data.

Personal Microsoft account holders are left in an even worse state: Planner isn't available to them, including Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscribers. Microsoft's advice is to choose another task-management app and prepare to export their data. Export instructions are still to come, and exporting won't necessarily produce something another app can import.

Very much a case of "don't let the door hit you on the way out."

Unifying tasks and plans is a good idea – the current situation does create confusion, as Microsoft acknowledged. However, taking an axe to To Do, which was developed to be a successor to Wunderlist (acquired in 2015 for a figure between $100 million and $200 million, an early action under Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella), seems extreme.

Microsoft calls the replacement "a unified platform for people and agents across Microsoft 365" and stated: "This unified platform makes accessing Planner through Copilot, Cowork and Autopilot easier."

Some users responding to the announcement were unimpressed, with one declaring "What a mess," and another asking if To Do might be spun off into an open source project: "Not everything needs to be put into an AI/Copilot agent."

Indeed, it doesn't. But a useful service that doesn't ram Copilot and AI integration down customers' throats at every opportunity? That would never do.

The message for To Do users appears to be: Get with the Plan(ner) or just get out. ®

The duck population at Naini Lake in Uttarakhand’s Nainital has fallen sharply over the past decade, with only a dozen birds remaining as rats prey on their eggs and disrupt their breeding cycle, raising concerns over the lake’s biodiversity, officials and residents said.

articles.title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
articles.text:
Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste. 

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.

“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.   

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks. 

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted. 

Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.  

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.  

While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”

Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.

Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.  

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”  

He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”  

“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”

articles.text:
Stalin calls Tamil Nadu ‘Vice City’ under CM Vijay, then comes cops' GTA-themed post
Tamil Nadu Police shared two anti-drug posters, showing arrests, drug seizures and awareness drives, using GTA-style artwork.
DMK chief M K Stalin on Thursday accused the Vijay-led TVK government of allowing Tamil Nadu to become a hub for drug trafficking, likening the state to ‘Vice City’, a fictional world in the Grand Theft Auto (GTA) series. Some time later, the Tamil Nadu Police posted two Grand Theft Auto (GTA)-themed posters showing its anti-narcotics operations in the state.
The development came on the day GTA VI, the latest instalment in the popular video game series, was released worldwide after a 13-year wait. Vice City is a fictional, crime-ridden city inspired by 1980s Miami, where players engage in gang wars, drug trafficking, robberies and other criminal activities.
The police shared the graphics on social media with the message, "Say no to drugs. Stand for a better tomorrow." The first poster, titled ‘Grand Theft Demolisher’, shows a police officer standing beside a patrol vehicle as three handcuffed suspects are taken away. It features a pink-and-purple sunset backdrop similar to the one used in GTA: Vice City and carries the tagline: "You only do what happens in the game, never in the real world".
Deep Dive
The second graphic, designed around a ‘Drive Against Drugs’ emblem, depicts various policing activities, including arrests, narcotics seizures, tracking of trafficking networks through digital maps and anti-drug awareness sessions for students.
Why Stalin called Tamil Nadu ‘Vice City’
“With the continued deterioration of law and order, alleged sexual misconduct by TVK members, major robberies and horrifying custodial deaths, Tamil Nadu is turning into a Vice City under TVK rule,” Stalin said on Thursday.
The remarks came after the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) seized 70 kg of heroin worth ₹140 crore from a vehicle during a check in Chennai's Madhavaram on Thursday. Two people were arrested in connection with the seizure.
On X, the former chief minister shared a satirical graphic titled ‘TVK Vice City’, modelled on the signature cover art of the popular video game. The collage featured illustrated portraits resembling Vijay and a TVK functionary, alongside images of narcotics, syringes, a crime scene and a person behind bars.
The graphic also featured news clips about recent controversies, including the National Commission for Women seeking an explanation from the DGP and a November 9 report about a man who alleged that he was forced to record a video statement.
Stalin also pointed out that the DRI had seized drugs worth ₹270 crore in Nagapattinam last month from a network allegedly linked to a TVK functionary.
Questioning the state police's efforts to stop drug trafficking, Stalin asked why major drug seizures were being made by a central agency instead of the Tamil Nadu Police.
"Are they unable to catch them, or are they turning a blind eye?" he asked.
He alleged that Tamil Nadu, once known as a leading destination for investors, was now becoming a "favourite destination" for methamphetamine and heroin smugglers.
Stalin also criticised the state's Director General of Police (DGP), accusing him of using crime statistics shared a day earlier to divert public attention.
He said simply announcing that "a case has been registered" after every incident was not enough. He also questioned why the police and the 65 special task force teams set up to fight drug trafficking had failed to catch the smugglers.
The DMK chief further raised concerns over robberies, custodial deaths and alleged misconduct by TVK workers, claiming that law and order had worsened in the state.
"With so many issues unfolding in the Home Department under Chief Minister Vijay's control, when will he speak if not now?" Stalin asked.
Dhinakaran questions TVK's anti-drug efforts
AMMK general secretary T T V Dhinakaran also criticised the state government over the heroin seizure. He questioned why the Tamil Nadu Police's narcotics enforcement teams were not doing what the Centre's DRI was doing to catch drug smugglers.
He asked the government to stop "releasing reels for publicity" and take strict action against drug trafficking gangs.
"It is a shame that the incompetent TVK government, which has completely failed to control the movement of drugs in various forms such as pills, injections, and chocolates, rendering the future of the younger generations bleak, is targeting journalists instead and using the 'Virtual Warriors' to abuse members of opposition parties on social media," Dhinakaran said in a statement.
He also said that anti-drug rallies and awareness banners on roads would not solve the problem. He urged Vijay to focus on taking action against drug trafficking networks.
PM Modi uses GTA VI release to highlight India's progress
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi also referred to the GTA VI release to highlight India's development over the past 13 years.
In 10 slides shared on Instagram and other social media platforms on Thursday, Modi compared India's progress between the release of GTA V in 2013 and GTA VI in 2026.
"India is playing a whole new game," he wrote, sharing the slides with the title ‘Between GTA V and VI, here's how’.
The slides highlighted India's growth as the world's fastest-growing major economy, poverty reduction, the completion of the sanitation mission, an increase in solar energy capacity, the growth of startups in the space sector, wider electrification and higher defence exports. They also mentioned improvements in maoist-affected districts.

articles.title: Japan to use Indian ranges for missile tests as New Delhi-Tokyo move to boost defence ties
articles.text:
New Delhi: Japan has announced that its Self-Defence Forces will begin using Indian firing ranges next year to test long-range missiles, following the conclusion of meetings between the foreign ministers and defence ministers of the two countries Thursday for the 2+2 Dialogue in Tokyo.
India has also raised its expectation for early consideration of the agreements related to co-production of the UNICORN (Unified Complex Radio) naval antenna. The first agreement on the co-production of UNICORN was announced earlier this year by Prime Minister Narendra Modi during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s visit to New Delhi in July.
The Joint Statement issued following the 2+2 Dialogue highlighted the expectation for Acceptance of Necessity for the UNICORN naval radio antenna by February 2027.
“This 2+2 meeting takes place at a time when the global order is being subjected to multiple shocks. There are two major ongoing conflicts whose impact have been felt even in distant regions. Coupled with the growing economic volatility and the after effects of the Covid pandemic, there are very strong concerns about energy, trade, food and health security. As we seek to secure ourselves on these fronts, trusted and substantive partnerships like ours become more valuable,” S. Jaishankar, India’s External Affairs Minister said in a statement to the press, following the 2+2 Dialogue.
He added, “Our 2+2 meeting naturally took into account the changing nature of warfare. We are witnessing the effective application of smart weapons and innovative solutions. Our cooperation here feeds into a larger engagement on innovation and startups. The big picture that our cooperation seeks to support is a multi-polar Asia and a multi-polar world.”
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh highlighted that he and his counterpart Shinjirō Koizumi “concurred” in moving forward to “swiftly realise concrete cooperation in fields of maritime and air domain awareness, search and rescue and information sharing agreements”.
He said, “We expressed our expectations for the early consideration of the UNICORN-related agreements and look forward to further strengthening our defence industrial cooperation under the framework of ‘Design with Japan and Make in India’.”
The Indian Defence Minister also highlighted the “need” for early conclusion of a maritime ship repair arrangement, which would allow for reciprocal provisions of ship repair facilities. Additionally, Singh underlined that niche technologies, underwater technologies and space domain awareness was also discussed. The two ministers agreed to “enhance” cooperation in anti-mine measures as well.
The major announcement of Japanese Self-Defence Forces using Indian testing ranges was made by Koizumi in a statement on X.
“We agreed that next year, the Self-Defense Forces will use an Indian firing range for the first time. This is also a major step strategically,” he wrote.

Last month, the Japanese Ground Self-Defence Force Chief of Staff General Masayoshi Arai had confirmed to local media that officials had been dispatched to India to inspect possible testing ranges for training with the Type-25 surface-to-ship missile. This missile has a range of roughly 1,000 kilometres.
“They welcomed the signing of LOI (Letter of Intent) toward the utilisation of firing ranges in India, whereby Japan Self-Defence Forces would, for the first time, conduct live-fire training etc., including those involving surface-to-ship missiles, at firing ranges in India,” Thursday’s Joint Statement read.
On Wednesday, Singh and Koizumi toured the Japanese Maritime Self-Defence Forces base at Yokosuka. Singh inspected the Mogami-class frigate JS Natori.
Jaishankar and Singh co-chaired the 2+2 Dialogue Thursday. The Indian External Affairs Minister reached Tokyo Wednesday, following his two-day visit to Manila alongside Prime Minister Narendra Modi for the India-ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) summit.
Singh and Koizumi have met three times in the last three months. They had met in New Delhi in August, and in Cebu, the Philippines last month on the margins of the ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus. The intensification of high-level meetings points to growing strategic convergences between New Delhi and Tokyo.
Jaishankar also held the India-Japan Foreign Ministers’ Strategic Dialogue during his visit to Tokyo, along with his Japanese counterpart Toshimitsu Motegi.
Apart from the 2+2 Dialogue, the two countries also launched a commemorative logo representing 75 years of the establishment of diplomatic ties, which will be celebrated in 2027.

China’s looming shadow
For Japan, India has increasingly become key to its strategic agenda as ties with China continue to remain tense. Japanese PM Takaichi travelled to China’s Shenzhen Wednesday to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, following her two-day visit to the Philippines for ASEAN-related summits.
However, China has sought to recast Japan’s recent military build-up as one that has potential to “destabilise Asia”, according to a report by The New York Times.
China and Japan have been in a war of words, especially after Takaichi announced that Japan may be forced to defend Taiwan—the self-governing territory, recognised by India as Chinese territory—in case of any future invasion by China.
Takaichi has moved to loosen export rules for military weapons, and increased defence spending to two percent of Japan’s gross domestic product (GDP) about two-years earlier than planned. In the looming shadow extended by Beijing, New Delhi has sought to describe its relationship with Tokyo as one that has an important role for stability across the Indo-Pacific.
“We also spoke about a growing tendency to weaponise connectivity, resources, services, supply chains and market shares. Many of these have direct implications for our national security. Strengthening resilience and exploring new options must be seen in that context. Concerns about connectivity and chokepoints have grown in the light of experiences in the Gulf,” said Jaishankar in his remarks to the press.
“We are two significant nations of the Indo-Pacific with a long and continuous history of friendship and goodwill. As we enter an era where each nation has to step-up its contributions to the global order, a stronger India-Japan relationship can certainly play a more important role. Our 2+2 discussions today and the understanding we reached were a very good step in that direction.”
As the war of words between China and Japan intensified this year, Beijing has imposed a number of export restrictions on merchandise flowing to Tokyo, pointing to the “weaponisation” of resources and supply chains. One of the earliest export restrictions on rare earth elements (REEs) was imposed by China in 2010 on exports to Japan, following a boat collision in the disputed territory of Senkaku islands.

articles.title: Cyberattack on service provider exposes payee data at 40 Irish credit unions
articles.text:
An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the company's delay in notifying them.

Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, said the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days.

Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable."

News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday.

Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6.

Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days.

The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them.

The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types:

  • Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames

  • Business Identifier Codes (BICs)

  • International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs)

  • Sort codes

  • Payment references

  • Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers

  • Payee addresses

Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds.

St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach.

The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the company notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data."

He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.

Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations.

"We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses."

Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services.

Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy said.

Credit unions operate similarly to traditional banks, offering savings accounts and loans, but are owned by their members and are not-for-profit organizations.

Troy told RTÉ that cybersecurity is a constant challenge for financial institutions, as technology and threats evolve over time.

"What's most important is that financial institutions take all the right measures to mitigate against these threats and that is what is happening," he said.

Separately, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, Prudential Regulation Authority, and Bank of England opened a joint consultation on cyber resilience guidance on Thursday.

The FCA said October brought its second-highest monthly tally of reported cyber incidents in five years, and the highest in 18 months. The proposed guidance clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements rather than introducing new rules. ®

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. articles.title: TfL takes Oyster photocard website offline after attackers compromise customer accounts
articles.text:
Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers.

The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise.

"We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," said Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident."

TfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did.

TfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected.

Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over.

Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too.

TfL says it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems.

Existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action. There's no word yet on when it'll be back.

"We hope to restore the affected website services as quickly as possible," Verma said.

TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised.

Two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement action against TfL, having deemed its response proportionate. There's nothing at present to suggest the two incidents are related.

Londoners can at least rest assured that their Oyster photocards still work. Whether the information they handed over to obtain them is in someone else's hands is another matter. ®

articles.title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
articles.text:
After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.

We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.  

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.)

I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.” 

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

articles.title: Sticky note on monitor provided keys to the company’s kingdom
articles.text:
Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note.

Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see.

During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not.

"Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door."

Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee.

Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries.

The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically.

The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records.

"At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said.

After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in.

The lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information.

"The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®
